title: Badminton
description: Signature badminton is taught as footwork before power. A student learns the split step, the chasse, and the lunge, then the clear, then the drop, because a smash hit from a poor position is a gift to the opponent. Our coaches feed multi-shuttle drills until movement is automatic, and deception is taught late, only when basic shots are reliable. Doubles rotation is drilled as a partnership skill, with partners learning to cover each other without words. The hall's praise goes to the player who reaches every shuttle in balance, not the player who smashes hardest.

demo.code:
ITEMS = [('Split steps', 40), ('Chasse steps', 30), ('Lunges', 24), ('Clears', 30), ('Drops', 20)]
print('Signature badminton drill counts')
total = 0
for name, val in ITEMS:
    total += val
    print('%s: %s' % (name, val))
print('Total: %s' % total)
print('Average: %.2f' % (total / len(ITEMS)))
demo.expected_output:
Signature badminton drill counts
Split steps: 40
Chasse steps: 30
Lunges: 24
Clears: 30
Drops: 20
Total: 144
Average: 28.80

training: Sessions pair footwork drills, multi-shuttle feeding, shot practice, and match play.
techniques: Signature basics are the split step, chasse, lunge, clear, and drop, in that order.
safety: Courts are kept clear, eye protection is advised for doubles, and warm-ups precede all play.
history: The Signature school follows badminton from battledore games to Olympic competition.

title: Squash
description: Signature squash is taught as length before trickery. A student learns to hit a straight rail deep to the back, then to return to the T, then to vary height, before any drop or boast is attempted, because a player who cannot hit length cannot build a rally. Our coaches drill movement to the T until it is automatic, and ghosting drills rehearse court movement without a ball. Drops are taught as a reward for good length, not as a first shot. The hall's praise goes to the player whose rails are straight and deep, rally after rally.

demo.code:
DAYS = [('Monday rails and T movement', 60), ('Wednesday ghosting', 30), ('Friday drops and boasts', 45), ('Saturday match play', 60)]
print('Signature squash training week')
total = sum(m for _, m in DAYS)
best = max(DAYS, key=lambda d: d[1])
for day, m in DAYS:
    print('%s: %d minutes' % (day, m))
print('Weekly total: %d minutes' % total)
print('Daily average: %.1f minutes' % (total / len(DAYS)))
print('Longest session: %s (%d minutes)' % (best[0], best[1]))
demo.expected_output:
Signature squash training week
Monday rails and T movement: 60 minutes
Wednesday ghosting: 30 minutes
Friday drops and boasts: 45 minutes
Saturday match play: 60 minutes
Weekly total: 195 minutes
Daily average: 48.8 minutes
Longest session: Monday rails and T movement (60 minutes)

training: Sessions pair rail drills, T movement, ghosting, and match play, with drops added only after length is reliable.
techniques: Signature basics are the straight rail, the return to the T, the cross-court, and then the drop.
safety: Eye protection is always worn, and players call lets rather than playing through interference.
history: The Signature school follows squash from Harrow School to the professional tour and the Olympics.

title: Table Tennis
description: Signature table tennis is taught as spin reading before spin making. A student learns to watch the opponent's paddle, to push and block reliably, and to move their feet, before any loop is attempted, because a player who cannot read spin cannot return it. Our coaches feed multi-ball drills until the forehand and backhand drives are automatic, and serves are practised as a daily habit, with one new serve learned each week. The hall's praise goes to the player who returns everything calmly, not the player who attacks everything wildly.

title: Padel
description: Signature padel is taught as walls before winners. A student learns to let the ball come off the glass, to lob when pushed back, and to hold position with a partner, before any smash is attempted, because padel is won by patience more than power. Our coaches drill doubles positioning until partners move as one, covering the middle without discussion. The bandeja, a controlled overhead that keeps position, is taught before the vibora, which attacks. The hall's praise goes to the pair that never leaves a gap, rally after rally.

demo.code:
QA = [('What stays in play in padel?', 'The walls: the ball may rebound off them after bouncing on the court.'), ('How are serves made?', 'Underarm.'), ('What is a bandeja?', "A controlled overhead shot that keeps the player's position."), ('What wins padel rallies most often?', 'Patience, positioning, and wall play, more than power.')]
print('Signature padel quiz')
for q, a in QA:
    print('Q: %s' % q)
    print('A: %s' % a)
print('Questions: %d' % len(QA))
demo.expected_output:
Signature padel quiz
Q: What stays in play in padel?
A: The walls: the ball may rebound off them after bouncing on the court.
Q: How are serves made?
A: Underarm.
Q: What is a bandeja?
A: A controlled overhead shot that keeps the player's position.
Q: What wins padel rallies most often?
A: Patience, positioning, and wall play, more than power.
Questions: 4

training: Sessions pair wall-rebound drills, doubles positioning, lob practice, and match play.
techniques: Signature basics are wall rebounds, the lob, doubles positioning, and the bandeja.
safety: Courts are checked for glass and surface, warm-ups precede play, and partners communicate before moving.
history: The Signature school follows padel from Corcuera's Mexican court to worldwide professional play.

title: Pickleball

A student learns to dink softly, to drop the third shot into the kitchen, and to move as a pair, before any drive is attempted, because pickleball is won at the net, not from the baseline. Our coaches drill dinking until soft hands are automatic, and they teach patience explicitly: the pair that waits for a high ball wins more than the pair that attacks every ball. The hall's praise goes to the pair whose dinks never rise, rally after rally.

title: Racquetball
description: Signature racquetball is taught as ceiling before kill. A student learns the ceiling ball, which buys time and resets a rally, then passing shots, then pinch shots, and only then the kill shot, because a kill attempted without position is a setup for the opponent. Our coaches drill court positioning until the player returns to centre after every shot, and eye protection is treated as part of the uniform, not an option. The hall's praise goes to the player whose ceiling balls are high and deep, rally after rally.

title: Basque Pelota

A student learns to read a rebound, to position for it, and to strike softly, with a soft ball on a short court, before any hard ball or cesta is used, because the wall decides every rally. Our programme teaches hand pelota first, since the hand teaches touch directly, and other modalities only when wall reading is reliable. Helmets are worn whenever a hard ball is in play, without exception. The hall's praise goes to the player whose rebounds are read early and struck calmly.

title: Jai Alai

A student learns to catch a soft ball in the cesta, to swing smoothly, and to read a rebound, on a short court, before any hard ball is used, because a throw without a clean catch is only a fumble at speed. Our programme teaches the continuous catch-and-throw motion slowly, with a partner feeding gentle rebounds, and speed is added only when the motion survives it. Helmets are worn from the first session, and the hall's praise goes to the player whose motion never breaks, even when the ball comes fast.

title: Real Tennis

A student learns the court's features by walking it, naming each wall, gallery, and opening, before any rally, because a player who does not know the court cannot use it. Our programme teaches the serve with cut first, since the serve shapes every point, and wall rebounds second, with rallies built slowly. Chases are taught as a game within the game, and the hall's praise goes to the player who uses the court cleverly, not the player who hits hardest.

Our programme teaches doubles positioning early, since doubles is the sport's most social form, and drop shots are drilled as a placement skill, not a trick. The hall's praise goes to the player whose rallies last longest and whose placements are kindest to their own position.

Sun protection and water breaks are treated as part of training, not interruptions. The hall's praise goes to the pair that moves lightest on sand.

title: Speedminton

A student learns to clear the speeder deep into the square, to move between squares, and to drop only when the opponent is pushed back, because a drop hit too early is easily returned. Our sessions use glowing speeders for evening play, which students love, and doubles is taught as shared squares with clear calls. The hall's praise goes to the player whose clears are deep and whose drops are timed, not the player who hits hardest.

Our sessions pair players of different levels deliberately, so stronger players learn to feed a rally rather than finish it. Competitive forms are offered as an option, but the hall's praise goes to the pair with the longest rally, not the pair with the most winners.

The hall's praise goes to the pair whose rally looks like a dance: fast, rhythmic, and unbroken.
